prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The five frames show a close work area: a large board/panel and the camera wearer’s torso/hands dominate the foreground at roughly 0.2–0.8 m, while the table saw/workbench is ahead-left at about 0.8–1.5 m and the floor, cabinets, and workshop structure extend behind it beyond roughly 1.5–3 m. Bright depth regions make the wearer’s hands, forearms, and the handled board easier to separate from the darker bench and background than in RGB; the board shifts from centered and partly upright to left/front, then drops or moves out of the central view as both hands come together in front of the torso. Across the strip, the wearer’s hands remain within arm’s reach, alternately extending forward and drawing inward, while the saw/workbench stays relatively fixed, indicating mostly hand/object and viewpoint rotation rather than a large approach or retreat through the room. The map suggests the nearer hand and board often occlude the torso and portions of the bench, with several surfaces continuing beyond the upper and side borders. Metric distances are only rough because this is monocular relative depth: the torso is sometimes rendered almost as near as the hands, sharp depth changes around the board and arms are inconsistent, and dark background regions may be compressed or missing.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation primarily separates the camera wearer’s visible torso, arms, and hands as one or more “person” masks in the lower and central foreground, roughly 0.2–0.8 m away, while most of the fixed workshop layout—saw, board, floor, cabinets, and walls—remains unlabeled. The person mask shows that the wearer occupies the viewpoint and faces generally forward/down toward the work area, but it cannot establish gaze; no clearly separate second person is consistently segmented. In the final frame it additionally labels a book-like object above-left of the hands and a cellphone-like object at upper-right, both apparently within the wearer’s reach and close to each other, although the RGB suggests these labels may be misclassifications of the handled workpiece or tools. Across frames, the mask tracks the arms moving from the left/center toward a more symmetric position in front of the torso and exposes changing self-occlusions where hands overlap the board and body. It clarifies object/person boundaries that are visually cluttered in RGB, but fragmented masks, changing person colors/instances, missing workshop objects, and questionable “book” and “cellphone” labels make precise layout, facing, and distance unreliable.
descriptions.pose: The pose map localizes the camera wearer’s hands against an otherwise empty field: magenta hand skeletons move from the left foreground in frame 1 to upper-center in frame 2, disappear or become confused with a yellow limb trace near center in frame 3, reappear right-of-center in frame 4, and become partly clipped near the upper-right edge in frame 5. These keypoints show finger/hand orientation and overlap more clearly than RGB, indicating hands repeatedly extend away from the torso and then come together or cross while remaining within the wearer’s arm’s reach, approximately 0.3–0.8 m from the camera. Sparse yellow body keypoints suggest portions of an arm rather than a complete second person; the wearer’s torso, head, gaze direction, and any other people are not sufficiently represented to determine facing or interpersonal distances. The map also makes partial out-of-view geometry explicit—especially the final-frame arm/hand continuing beyond the right border—and shows occlusion when one hand or the held object hides joints. It is unreliable for full-scene layout and metric range because most body joints and all workshop objects are absent, hand identities/colors are not stable, and several skeletons are incomplete or anatomically distorted.
